subject: Ward Protocols
title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Fluids, Potassium and Insulin — Clinical Logic
preview: DKA requires recognition of ketosis and metabolic acidosis, careful fluid replacement and potassium-aware insulin therapy.

sections.title: Recognize the biochemical syndrome
points: Assess clinical hydration, mental status, respiratory effort and any precipitating infection or missed insulin.
Do not rely on blood glucose alone: some DKA cases present without very high glucose, particularly with SGLT2-inhibitor exposure.

sections.title: Follow the physiological priorities
points: Fluid resuscitation, potassium assessment and insulin are linked decisions; marked potassium depletion must be addressed before insulin is started.
Use a locally approved adult or pediatric protocol for rates, concentrations and potassium replacement.

sections.title: Avoid early treatment errors
points: Insulin can move potassium into cells and precipitate dangerous hypokalemia if potassium deficits are overlooked.
A falling glucose reading does not establish correction of ketoacidosis; ongoing dextrose may be required as insulin continues.

quickRevision: DKA is defined by a compatible diabetes or hyperglycemia context, ketonemia and metabolic acidosis; euglycemic presentations can occur.
Restore circulation, assess serum potassium and start appropriate insulin treatment with frequent monitoring.
Glucose may improve before ketoacidosis resolves; assess resolution using ketones and the acid–base picture.

quiz.question: What must be assessed and corrected alongside insulin during DKA treatment?
quiz.explanation: Potassium status. Fluid resuscitation, potassium assessment and insulin are linked decisions; marked potassium depletion must be addressed before insulin is started.
